speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: It will also allow ICA to provide more convenient registration services to the public and to enhance security in Singapore.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Currently, ICA collects photographs and fingerprints from Singapore Citizens (SCs) and Permanent Residents (PRs) as personal identifiers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: These are collected during the National Registration Identity Card (NRIC) registration and re-registration process.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: As technology improves, other forms of personal identifiers may be used to complement existing identifiers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: These new personal identifiers are restricted to images, measurements or recordings of an external part of a person's body; or measurements or recordings of a person's voice.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: These personal identifiers will not involve the taking of body samples obtained through invasive means, such as blood samples.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: This has been included in the Schedule, along with photographs and fingerprints currently collected by ICA.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: To ensure that the collection of iris images will be easy and convenient, it will be collected as part of the NRIC registration and re-registration process.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Iris images will also be collected as part of the passport application or renewal process.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: It has been in use in countries, such as Germany and the Netherlands, since the early 2000s.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Passport holders from European Union countries can voluntarily enrol their iris images with German and Dutch immigration authorities as well.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Once this is done, immigration clearance to enter these countries through some major airports can be done using iris images.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Authorities can verify the identities of these travellers by comparing their iris images against what had been previously enrolled.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Some other countries, like the United Arab Emirates (UAE), have also mandated the collection of iris images from their citizens to facilitate immigration clearance.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: UAE mandated collection of iris images from all citizens since 2013.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: The enrolled iris images are used to verify the identity of citizens when they travel in and out of the country.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Page: 35 The collection and verification of iris images are similar to taking a photograph.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: It is convenient, contactless and non-intrusive and can be completed in seconds.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: The use of iris scan technology will augment current identity verification methods using photographs and fingerprints.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: A person's fingerprints may also wear out over time as he gets older, or if he does a lot of manual work.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: ICA has received feedback from some travellers who found it difficult to use the automated clearance gates at the checkpoints.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Poor fingerprint quality could also be a reason.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: These travellers had to be directed to the manned counters instead.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: This has been a source of intrigue and, sometimes, even frustration to these travellers and also to fellow travellers queuing up behind them to use the automated lanes.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: The use of iris scan technology can help reduce such problems by providing an additional avenue for persons to verify their identity.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Once implemented, persons can continue to use ICA's automated facilities at the checkpoints, even if their fingerprints may have faded over time.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: This will smoothen the immigration clearance process for individuals and also benefit other travellers, by reducing overall queue times.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: The end result is more efficient and effective immigration clearance at our checkpoints.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Clause 5 sets down the mandatory and discretionary rules concerning the name of a person to be entered into the national register.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Clause 16 makes a related amendment to the Registration of Births and Deaths Act (RBDA) concerning the registration of a child's name at birth.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Most individuals and parents try their best to come up with good and meaningful names for themselves or their children.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: The vast majority of names are thus registered with no issue.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: However, ICA has, from time to time, received requests to register names that are inappropriate.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: These situations are not common, but they happen.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Inappropriate names include names that may be impractical, names that may be offensive, or names that may be confusing or misleading.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Clause 5 makes it mandatory for a name to be expressed using the modern English alphabet, though it may include one or more permitted characters gazetted under the new section 9A(2) of the RBDA.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Without this, individuals could attempt to register names which are composed of non-English characters or even numerals or punctuation marks.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Many people will find it very difficult to pronounce or read these names.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: They can cause difficulties in identifying the individual which may result in practical inconveniences or even security risks.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: The length of a name must also not exceed the character limit of ICA's systems.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: The current character limit is already long, at 66 characters.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: We have to be practical and impose a limit on the length of names.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Otherwise, names that are too long would be truncated in official documents and could lead to potential misidentification, posing security risks.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Such names are misleading and could potentially cause confusion.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: The Commissioner will carefully consider the Page: 36 circumstances of each case, before he exercises his discretionary powers of refusal to register the names.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: The third area of amendments makes clear ICA's powers to appoint non-ICA employees as registration officers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Clause 3 of the Bill sets out the classes of persons that the Commissioner can appoint as registration officers for the purposes of the Act, or any particular provision of the Act.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: These include public officers, employees of public authorities and employees of prescribed institutions.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Prescribed institutions have to be specified by the Minister in the subsidiary legislation and can include private entities.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: The amendments will allow the Commissioner to appoint non-ICA employees as registration officers for any particular provision of the Act.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: This will allow ICA to partner other Government agencies or private entities to deliver certain registration services more conveniently to the public and at more locations.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: ICA will only allow non-ICA employees to perform very specific functions, which will be carefully selected and tightly scoped.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Once collected, these images will be directly transmitted and stored in ICA's database.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Non-ICA employees will not have access to individual personal records in ICA's database.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: ICA has considerable experience partnering external agencies in this manner, with the necessary safeguards on security and privacy.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Currently, ICA already partners SingPost to deliver some services to Singaporeans.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: These include alternate site collection of identity cards and passports.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: For instance, ICA officers will be empowered to seize suspicious identity cards and to perform related investigations.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Clauses 8, 9 and 10 of the Bill provide registration officers with additional enforcement powers, as well as new powers to investigate offences under the Act.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Providing ICA officers with these powers will serve to improve ICA's effectiveness in the administration of the entire spectrum of NRA-related issues, from the issuance of NRIC to the enforcement and investigation of offences under the NRA.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Clause 8 introduces new sections 15A and 15B.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: The new section 15A gives registration officers the powers to take possession of any document suspected to be false or invalid, when such a document is produced during registration or alteration of a person's particulars in the national register.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: The new section 15B gives registration officers and Police officers the powers to demand the surrender of a suspicious identity card.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: This includes cards that are suspected to have been obtained under false or misleading information; or been used in the commission of offences under the NRA; or been issued or altered by any unauthorised party.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Page: 37 Clause 9 amends section 16 to give registration officers the powers to conduct searches under this Act.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Clause 10 introduces new sections 16A, 16B and 16C.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Section 16A, in particular, requires registration officers to comply with the Criminal Procedure Code when making arrests.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Section 16B gives registration officers powers to investigate offences under the Act, whereas section 16C allows for registration officers to initiate criminal proceedings by issuing a notice to the suspected offender to attend Court.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: For example, the Commissioner cannot appoint registration officers with powers under sections 15B, 16, 16B and 16C, concerning the surrender of identity cards, arrest, search and investigation, unless they are public officers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: In addition, we intend to grant such powers only to ICA officers and not to any public officer.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: The above amendments will serve to improve ICA's effectiveness in the administration of the entire spectrum of NRA-related issues.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: The collection of additional personal identifiers, such as iris images, will also enhance Singapore's security through strengthening the identification of individuals.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: However, I have some questions regarding some of the changes.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: As a former Police officer, I am deeply aware of the various threats that Singapore may face, especially from those abroad who seek to infiltrate our country to cause harm and destruction.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Therefore, I am supportive of the amendments proposed for the Act, which aim to strengthen the effectiveness and efficiency of our border security operations.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: How will ICA make the collection of iris scans more convenient for those who may not see the need to register, such as those who do not travel out of Singapore often or at all, or those who are not able to visit the collection centres during normal working hours due to their work arrangements?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: While the collection and identification of the iris images are contactless and non-intrusive physically, the idea that the Government is collecting iris scans is new to many Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Residents have asked me how personal data, such as fingerprints and iris images, can be protected from being lost or misused.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Can the Minister, therefore, elaborate on measures to safeguard these Page: 38 personal data?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Also, how will ICA educate the public on the purpose and need to gather iris scans and assure them of the protection of data?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Due to the scale of this exercise, it may not be practical for ICA to depend solely on its officers to register thousands of residents on a daily basis.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: A more effective way is to tap on personnel from the public and private sectors by appointing them as registration officers, so that more locations can be made available for the collection of iris scans.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Can the Minister, therefore, clarify on the roles and powers of registration officers from the private sector?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Thirdly, what measures would there be to ensure the registration officers protect the data collected and encrypt them in an appropriate manner?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Lastly, how can the public differentiate between registration officers from the private and public sectors?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: All registration officers must understand the importance of protecting these sensitive data and practise due diligence accordingly.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Clarifications to these questions would help us better understand the administrative and enforcement duties of these non-ICA registration officers.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Is there a specific timeframe for iris scans to be implemented at all our checkpoints?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Would iris scans eventually replace fingerprint technology or would that serve as an add-on?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: If so, would iris scans slow down the immigration clearance process, taking into consideration the varying volumes of travellers at our different checkpoints?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I look forward to the clarifications from the Minister.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: With that, Mdm Speaker, I support the Bill.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I do not oppose the thrust of the Bill but I have a number of queries about the context for the amendments and a few requests for clarification and assurance on how these provisions will be implemented.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: These penalties are relevant to low-income, multi-problem households.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: As an FSC volunteer in the past, I have met a number of low-income Singaporeans who have long lost their NRICs and who were deterred from seeking help from social work agencies and Government agencies by the prospect of having to pay for replacing their NRICs or, worse yet, Page: 39 charged with an offence they and their families will suffer as a result.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: An NRIC is crucial to interact with Government agencies to exercise the rights and responsibilities of a citizen.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Rather than risk deterring at-risk persons from coming forward to ask for help, would ICA consider adopting a similar approach to that taken by our public healthcare institutions?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: And that approach is that no one will be denied medical help because they cannot pay.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Next, Madam, I would like to speak about clause 5 which places some limitations on what names can be registered.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: As a matter of practical reality, of course, very few people would want to register a name longer than 66 characters.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I fully recognise that, but there would be some individuals and families who want to.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: If a family wants to give their child a name that is too long or someone wants to do a deed poll to the same effect, will they be given sufficient time to consider how to abbreviate their officially registered name to 66 characters?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In those days, people had to live with the results of that.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I hope that parents and individuals doing deed polls who find themselves on the wrong side of these new rules would have enough time and space to discuss alternatives with the registration officer, rather than being pressured to agree to an officially approved abbreviated version of their name, on the spot, as it were.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Since every act of legislation should be a response to a real-world problem or a problem that is likely to happen, my question is: have there been a significant or an increasing number of persons wanting to register their names that might be deemed to contain an impermissible reference to a rank or an award or deemed to be offensive or contrary to the national interest?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I would also like to question the terms "offensive" and "contrary to the public interest".

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: These are broad-sweeping terms that will give ICA very broad latitude in denying the registration of a name, setting up a tension with the right of individuals to choose their names and their children's names.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Could the Senior Minister of State cite some examples of names that will be contrary to the national interest that it has encountered or, at least, indicate broadly what types of names will these be?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Will these be, for example, names that contain expletives?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: If that is the case, if my understanding is correct, then, no doubt, this is possible when people replace their NRICs and passports.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: But for those who are not replacing their NRICs and passports Page: 40 anytime soon, what would be the logistics or undertaking in such a massive exercise of collecting iris scans from every Singaporean and PR?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: What would be the schedule associated with that?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Next, Madam, section 3(4)(c) allows the employee of a prescribed institution to act as a registration officer.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This opens the way for private corporations to perform national registration tasks on contract.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Would national registration officers working with private contractors, as with their public sector counterparts, be asked to sign the usual undertakings under the Official Secrets Act regarding the safeguarding of official information?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Also – and here I return to an issue I have raised in the House in another context – would the Ministry conduct a privacy impact assessment, or PIA, before outsourcing national registration functions to companies, given the highly sensitive nature of personal identifier information, including possibly iris scan information?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: And how highly sought after such data would be by criminal syndicates?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Also, the Bill does not expressly deal with contracts with the outsourcing contractors themselves.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Unlike private organisations, the Government is not bound by the Personal Data Protection Act (PDPA).

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In previous parliamentary debates over the PDPA, the Government has said that it is bound by its own internal rules.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The PDPA requires private organisations to ensure that organisations which process data on their behalf, or data intermediaries, comply with the PDPA protection and retention obligations.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Terms and conditions in its tenders should also take into account the PDPC's guidelines on this issue for private organisations.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Is this extension of Police powers really necessary or desirable?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Can Police officers simply perform these tasks on behalf of national registration agencies?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Lastly, and in conclusion, I have a technical question.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: If iris scanning technology is to be purchased and deployed on a considerable scale, would this not result in a considerable increase in financial expenditure?

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: There is a global movement in several countries to tighten registration and security.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: A prototype has run in India and it was used to capture biometric Page: 41 information from 300 children.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: In terms of the pertinent issues with regard to the Act, the Senior Minister of State has mentioned earlier the timeframe for rolling out the iris scans.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: This will take place at various stages when renewing your identity card or passport at border controls.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Related to that, the Senior Minister of State has also related its security implications.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Therefore, my second clarification lies with long-term visitors to Singapore ‒ whether they be workers, foreign workers, expatriates ‒ would it not be in the interest of security to also have this done for them?

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: The changes that are contained within the National Registration Bill are important.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: But there are, of course, some misguided Singaporeans who may view it as Orwellian measures designed to control Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: This is one perception that I think needs to be handled carefully and communicated effectively so that it would not have an impact on the Government's standing.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Education is essential and I hope the authorities will undertake the necessary measures to allay misconceptions and allegations of invasion of privacy.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: With regard to powers that are assigned to registration officers to investigate, could I clarify with the Senior Minister of State if there has been a recent increase in the number of offences that warrants a shift of investigative powers from the Police to ICA?

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Would there also be a transition period for this to take place?

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: With regard to names, registration officers currently at hospitals also undertake the registration of children's births.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Therefore, would ICA be training these registration officers with regard to the types of names that are allowed or not allowed, or will all names be permissible at registration but denied further downstream by the Registrar or Commissioner?

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Also, in terms of cultural sensitivities, under the Schedule, it is indicated that names that relate to titles or positions will be disallowed.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: But in certain cultures, titles are also born of alien names.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Under clause 3, as I have mentioned, the registration officers may change relatively often, depending on their employment with that particular organisation.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: How will ICA manage the appointment of registration officers that may go through some amount of flux?

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: A couple of years back, it was also reported in the local papers, and also then aired in the international media, about an individual with a name closely resembling that of a comic superhero.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Some joked that even his poor father's name seems to also represent.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: But in his cultural background, it appears that it is relatively common in Java.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: So, with regard to names that may appear offensive or may have long-term impact on a child, what are ICA's guidelines on these?

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Notwithstanding some of the clarifications that I have sought, I Page: 42 wholeheartedly support the Bill.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We have sufficient proof that iris imaging is far more accurate than all other biometric identifiers available today.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Compared to fingerprints, which can wear off, iris scans have a much lower chance of false matches.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: It has already been tried, tested and deployed in other parts of the world – from airports, to banks and smartphones.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This year, the UN started to use it to identify refugees.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: In the private sector, industry watchers also consider it the next big thing.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Thus, if new technology is available for a safer Singapore, then we must seize it – and I am encouraged that this Bill does reflect the Government's vigilance and eagerness to seize opportunities to strengthen security.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: That said, in order for us to reap the full benefits of this new technology, I would like to raise a few questions.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Iris scans are especially sensitive because they are so powerful.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The most advanced scanners can identify many people in a split second, even from a long-range.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The data is almost fool-proof and is permanent.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: If this data falls into the hands of people with mal-intentions, the consequences can be dangerous.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The public could have questions on how secure the database will be, whether third parties, apart from the Government, will have access to the data and so on.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: There will always be teething issues with the introduction of any new technology, especially one as personal as this, and we should have ready answers.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: In this light, can the Minister share plans on how it will ensure that the new data collected will be secure?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: How does the Ministry plan to satisfy the public about this?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Some people might be skeptical – even fearful – of new technology like this, which could be seen as a page out of a science fiction novel.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: For the older generation, there could be misconceptions ‒ will it hurt my eyes, does it involve lasers?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: For the younger generation, there could be discomfort from what they see as additional Government "surveillance".

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Certainly, the technology has been tried and tested, but how does the Ministry plan to educate the public to debunk these myths?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Thirdly, I would like to find out more about the technology deployed at the immigration checkpoints.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I have read that iris scanners are able to detect stress through indicators, such as movement of the eyeballs.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Once stress is detected, the system will immediately alert authorities.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: If this is truly available, it would be a real step-up for security at our checkpoints.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Minister share if the iris imaging technology we will acquire can provide this extra layer of security?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: My final point is to ask which Ministry and Government services will have access to, and use of the data.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Apart from immigration and perhaps, the Police, are there plans for schools, hospitals and other relevant services to also use the data for identification – perhaps not immediately, but in the Page: 43 longer term?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Iris scans have surely proven its effectiveness and I am in full support of it.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: But in order for us to reap its full benefits, I hope we have strict safeguards in place, particularly for data protection.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: It has been over two decades since the Act was last amended.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I agree that the various amendments proposed are necessary to update ICA's operations and to enhance the effectiveness and efficiency of our border controls.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The collection of iris images and, in some cases, recordings of voices, can help to strengthen our identity verification methods.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: It even works in the presence of clear contact lenses and non-mirrored glasses.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: In addition, there is also research suggesting that irises are susceptible to ageing effects that change their appearance over time.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Some researchers had already found a way to replicate such images, "creating the possibility of stealing someone's identity through their iris".

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Would the Minister share what measures we have in place to overcome these potential problems and threats to our new iris-recognition system?

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Next, I would like to state my support for the amendment to provide our ICA officers with the powers to investigate offences under the NRA.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: This would be much more efficient and effective than relying only on our Police officers to do so, as is currently the case.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The administration and operations would be more streamlined under this new arrangement.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: This would also free up our Police officers to focus on other criminal investigations.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Now, ICA will have the power to protect our young from offensive names, however rarely it occurs.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Although I support the Bill, I wish to highlight the need for robust and stronger safeguards with respect to privacy and security Page: 44 arising from the collection of biometric data.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: MHA says that iris scanning is "a proven technology" that is "convenient, contactless and non-intrusive".

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: I join Members who spoke earlier on their concerns on both counts of privacy and security.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: As scanning of irises is contactless and non-intrusive, the technology could potentially scan irises covertly, as opposed to the scanning of thumb prints, which requires active participation of the person being identified.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: These developments are perceived as Orwellian because they allow iris cameras to be unseen and to operate in a non-consensual surveillance mode.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Once an iris becomes a digital file, that file will need to be adequately protected against attack.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Systems can be hacked, biometric identifiers could be stolen and misused.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: What are the safeguards which have been and will be put in place to address these privacy and security concerns in collecting biometric data, such as iris scans?

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: How will these safeguards be communicated to the public to allay concerns?

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: I urge ICA to do this and at no cost impact to Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: This updating exercise will also help in the iris scan roll-out.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Mr Melvin Yong asked how and when iris scan technology will be implemented at the checkpoints and how this will affect the efficiency of the checkpoint clearance process.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: So, more Singaporeans and Permanent Residents will, therefore, enjoy automated clearance at our checkpoints, with the reduced need to be diverted to manned checkpoints.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: This will improve the overall efficiency and efficacy of our immigration clearance process.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Page: 45 Mr Louis Ng asked about whether iris scanners can detect stress through the movement of eyeballs, to bolster border security.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: While potentially useful, our sense is that this technology does not appear mature at present.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: We continue to look at all these methodologies and will make decisions as they mature.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: The collection and verification of iris images are very safe and will not harm our eyes, and the process is similar to taking a photograph ‒ convenient, contactless, non-intrusive and can be done within a matter of seconds.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Mr Alex Yam asked whether existing NRIC holders will be required to enrol their iris images and when ICA intends to begin doing so.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Mr Yong wanted to know if this process can be made convenient for the public.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: And Mr Leon Perera asked about when this iris enrolment can be done outside of these three phases – registration, re-registration and passport collection.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: To make it convenient for people, ICA will do this as part of ICA's existing interactions with the public.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: And these include compulsory NRIC registration and re-registration.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: So, there are two phases, one at 15 and one at 30, as well as during passport application and renewal process.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: There is, therefore, no need to make a separate trip to ICA Building just to have your iris image collected.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: So, we build it into the existing process and we collect it as and when people make use of ICA's existing services.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Mr Melvin Yong asked about how we will help people with disability or serious illness.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: The ICA Home Visit Team will enrol their biometric identifiers like iris images at their homes, when they register or re-register for their NRICs.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: This is an existing service, and all that the applicants need to do is provide documentary proof of their condition or their caregiver can do so on their behalf.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Mr Melvin Yong, Mr Louis Ng and Mr Patrick Tay asked how personal data will be protected and whether the information will be shared with third parties.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Only authorised ICA officers can access the database as part of their work.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Those caught misusing the data will be punished.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Second, sensitive data like fingerprint and iris images are encrypted before storage in a secure database.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Third, ICA servers are protected by physical and software measures, in line with international security standards.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Fourth, the National Registration Regulations tightly regulate and restrict the instances under which personal identifiers, such as fingerprints and iris images, may be shared.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Ms Joan Pereira said that iris patterns may be affected by cataract surgery and that these patterns may also change over time as a person ages.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: This is already the case today for fingerprints and photographs, facial features.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: So, for instance, fingerprints can fade with time or if the person does a lot of manual work.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: A person will also look different with age.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: So, if you register at 15 and when you are 30, the photograph will look different over time.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: The person can also alter physical appearance or assume a fake identity by replicating another person's fingerprints.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: For those whose iris images cannot be effectively scanned or enrolled due to medical reasons, such as cataracts, ICA will continue to rely on other identifiers, such as fingerprints or facial recognition, to identify such individuals.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Mr Melvin Yong also asked about people who wear very thick glasses.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: When we enrol iris images, we will request that they remove their glasses in order for the image scan to be more accurately scanned or enrolled.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Ms Joan Pereira asked if identity theft can be committed by replicating a person's iris patterns.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Like other biometric identifiers, it is certainly possible.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: But studies have shown that this requires very sophisticated equipment and is harder to do so accurately.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Biometric systems also have built-in mechanisms to ensure that the presented biometrics are authentic.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Carrying out identification using iris images alongside other existing identifiers will make the overall system more secure and robust and make identity theft harder to commit.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Having said that, we cannot be overly reliant on technology and the human dimension is still very important.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: We will continue to deploy our officers to look out for tell-tale signs or suspicious behaviour amongst travellers that may indicate a possible identity theft.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Mr Leon Perera asked about whether there would be processes beyond what I have just identified for the enrolment of irises.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: And, of course, when a person applies for a passport, there will also be another opportunity and touch-point to enrol the iris.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: This would necessarily mean that enrolment of the entire population will take quite some time.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: But let us start with the initial touch points first.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: That will already allow large numbers of Singaporeans and PRs to have their iris images enrolled.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: I will move on to the appointment of non-ICA employees as registration officers.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Mr Alex Yam and Mr Melvin Yong asked why non-ICA employees should be appointed as registration officers.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Mr Leon Perera asked whether these non-ICA employees would be subjected to the Official Secrets Act and other forms of security measures and undertakings.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Mr Alex Yam asked if this was a productivity measure.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: ICA will be highly selective about what we appoint non-ICA employees to do.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: These includes strict user-access controls to prohibit non-ICA employees from accessing, retrieving or altering any information, such as an individual's personal records, from ICA's systems.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Personal information collected by these employees will also be transmitted directly to ICA.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Non-ICA employees will not be allowed to edit the information.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Their role is to guide the public through the enrolment process and not to manage the information collected.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Page: 47 For greater accountability, ICA will only appoint full-time staff of these entities as registration officers.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Private entities will be required to submit to ICA the particulars of each employee whom they intend to appoint with these registration duties.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: And each of them will have to be individually appointed as a registration officer by the Commissioner of ICA.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: This will be done only after ICA has assessed the entity and each individual for their suitability, and conduct necessary screening measures.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: So, apart from the suitability of the institution and the individuals, Mr Leon Perera asked whether there will be a privacy impact assessment or security impact assessment conducted.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: The entire framework will be put under scrutiny in order to ensure that privacy is secured.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Every registration officer is required to produce an identification card or document as evidence of the officer's authority.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: And this will clearly state whether he is from the public sector or he is from one of these external entities that we appoint to carry out some of these functions.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: If he does not do so, members of the public are well advised not to comply with any order or demand by these individuals.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Mr Alex Yam said that parents should think of the consequences of giving undesirable names to their children and asked if ICA could come up with a set of guidelines on allowable names.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Mr Leon Perera wanted to know if time would be given to parents who register names that may not be registered under these new rules instead of being compelled to make a decision there and then, on the spot.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: I will deal first with Mr Leon Perera's point.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Certainly, this is a very important decision for parents and will affect the children all through their lives.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: The kind of names to give is not an issue that we expect parents to take lightly.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Neither do we want to put them in a position to be rushed.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: So, certainly, in the rare instance where the name suggested may not comply with the rules, the officers will give the parents ample time to reconsider.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Even with the registration of a child's birth, there is a period of time given to parents to make that registration.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: So, in response to Mr Leon Perera's question about how often we see such inappropriate names or names exceeding 66 characters, the answer is very few and far between.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: This is the power that is embedded in the registration legislation of many other developed countries.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: The legislative language referencing public interest also exists in these other countries.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: It is not our intention to regulate the kinds of names parents choose for their children.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Instead, ICA will assess each name at the point of registration to ensure that they do not flout the conditions stipulated in the new section 6A.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: And names that do not meet the mark will be refused registration.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: The Commissioner may also refuse to register names that are obscene or offensive.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: The Commissioner will have to carefully consider each case on its own merits before he exercises his discretionary powers to refuse registration, a power which ought to be exercised sparingly.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Mr Leon Perera asked for examples of names that could possibly flout public interest.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Those that used titles like "Sir", "Professor", "President"; names that are offensive or that use expletives.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: One other example could be names that could possibly be deemed derogatory or highly offensive to any particular race or religion.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Again, bearing in mind that this is the parents' right to express the kind of name they would like for their children to carry through Page: 48 their life, we will exercise these powers very sparingly and carefully.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: ICA considers each application for waiver holistically, taking into account a range of factors.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: The loss of an NRIC poses not just inconvenience to the individual but also tremendous risks to him or her in terms of identity theft.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: People could use their ICs to borrow from loan sharks.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Identity thefts could also pose national security risks.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Criminals, syndicates or even terrorist organisations could use Singapore identity documents or NRICs maliciously.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Therefore, it is important to reflect proper safekeeping of the NRIC in the law.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: We balance the need to emphasise that responsibility with the ability of people to afford the replacement fees.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: In relation to affordability, I have given the Member the answer that ICA will assess each case based on the person's circumstances and the circumstances under which the identity card was lost.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: ICA will release more details in due course.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Because when ICA puts the systems in place, MHA will include this amount as part of the Supply Bill and we will reflect that expenditure under that Bill.
